paragraphs: Fostering for Richmond's own children is provided by Achieving for Children, the not-for-profit organisation that runs children's services for the borough. The council's fostering page, updated in November 2026, says it looks after vulnerable children locally through emergency, short-term and long-term foster care, and it sends enquiries to Achieving for Children's fostering team. That service is shown above alongside the independent agencies that list Richmond upon Thames as an area they cover.

Finding enough local homes has long been a challenge in the borough. A placement sufficiency strategy written for Richmond and Kingston in 2015 said high housing costs and the space carers need made it especially hard to place brothers and sisters together, and it set out to recruit more carers in parts of Richmond with few fostering households, naming Kew, Barnes and East Sheen. Those figures are now old, so ask any service you speak to about the children it needs homes for today.

A carer writing on the council's website described the practical side: a spare bedroom, being around in the day or having flexible hours, some experience of looking after children, and financial stability. She added that age, disability, being single or having no children of your own do not stop you fostering, and that Achieving for Children was keen to hear from people open to caring for children of different ages.

Before you decide, talk to the council's service and to two or three of the agencies above, and ask each what it pays, how it trains new carers and who you can call out of hours. The Kingston upon Thames page lists more services close by.
